svg.text: Data models: one family, one notation
Every model below computes the same function. The same example runs through all of them: Alice and Bob, two files and a device.
ACCESS-CONTROL MATRIX
f(subject, action, resource) tabulated. Mostly empty, so nobody stores it.
Lampson, 1974 — subjects down one axis, objects across the other
reindex by column
reindex by row
ACCESS CONTROL LIST
store the relation by column, at the resource
exact and invertible — the matrix, transposed and nothing else
to give Bob everything Alice has, you visit every object
mutation: the owner (DAC)
CAPABILITY LIST
store the relation by row, at the subject
exact and invertible — the same information, transposed
to give Bob everything Alice has, you go to Alice
mutation: still the administrator
transpose
RBAC
factor the relation: subject → role → permission
exact — expand the roles and the matrix comes back
the saving is sharing the middle term, not changing which end the data hangs off
ABAC
do not tabulate — compute the relation, per request
exact — evaluate the predicate over every pair and the matrix comes back
context is a first-class argument here; a table has no axis for it
ReBAC
derive the relation from a graph of tuples
exact — run the check over every pair and the matrix comes back
a check asks: is the resource reachable from the subject along an allowed path?
smaller storage, easier administration, more work at request time
store
derive
the five above are notations for that rectangle. The one below is a different matrix.
OBJECT CAPABILITY — square the matrix
both axes range over the same set of entities. A cell reads: which of Y's operations may X invoke?
ACL and capability lists are the special case where the entity set splits in two,
so the bottom-left block is empty by construction and you may as well draw it rectangular.
Alice: rw File A is a true statement about what
Alice can eventually cause, and a false one about
the authority she holds. The path is the difference.

g.text: Bob is a row and a column. Alice → Bob → File A is two cells, not one,
and Bob may refuse, revoke, log, or forward only a subset.
The cell (Alice, Bob) asks whether Alice may talk to Bob at all —
a question a rectangular matrix has nowhere to put.
A mutation rule in the matrix's own terms
Alice may write into Bob's row only if her own row already reaches
both Bob and the thing she is granting. Authority moves along existing edges.
